newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia's Samper faces rough ride to succession.
newsitem.headline: Colombia's Samper faces rough ride to succession.

text.p: President Ernesto Samper, who calls himself the "quake-proof president" because he has endured so many calls for his resignation, can still joke about the dim view many Colombians have of him.
If he walked on water to save a boatload of drowning children, he told Reuters last week, the next day's headlines would read not "Miracle" but "Samper Can't Swim."

The 46-year-old Samper is known for his quirky sense of humour. But he conceded, just two weeks before the United States will decide whether to clamp painful economic sanctions on Colombia, that there was little to laugh about.

Since he took office, unlike any other time in Colombia's long-running guerrilla war, leftist rebels have proved they can attack anywhere at will, taking soldiers as hostages and kidnapping hundreds of civilians for exorbitant ransoms. About 60 soldiers taken prisoner in August are still being held and at least 16 others were killed in a lengthy battle with rebels just 30 miles (50 km) outside the capital this month.

"The armed forces are in complete control of Colombian territory," Samper said. But military commanders, who say privately the president lacks both credibility and authority because of the drug scandal that nearly forced him out of office last year, say their 100,000-man combat force -- nearly a third of which is devoted to guarding strategic oil and coal facilities and infrastructure -- is too small to cover Colombia's vast and often tortuous terrain.
At a recent luncheon for foreign journalists, army commander Gen. Manuel Jose Bonett showed a map illustrating "hot spots" of leftist guerrilla activity. The map covered almost all of Colombia.

Samper acknowledged that the rebels have become increasing powerful and said "Colombian democracy is threatened." Quoting intelligence reports, he said Colombia's largest rebel group made up to $700 million last year alone through the narcotics trade and the protection of rural drug operations.

In the interview Samper, who is serving his last full year as president, also said Colombia's economy was in excellent shape and poised for healthy growth this year. But poor tax collection and growing public spending forced him to declare a "state of economic emergency" in January to plug a widening fiscal deficit.
State workers began an indefinite strike last Tuesday to protest against pay hikes that fall way short of compensating for inflation of more than 21 percent last year.

Colombia was severely shaken last March when U.S. President Bill Clinton included the Andean nation on a list of virtual pariah states -- Afghanistan, Burma, Iran, Nigeria and Syria -- that had failed to cooperate in the international fight against drugs.

In an annual report required by Congress, Clinton will announce on Feb. 27 whether Colombia should be "certified" as a trustworthy ally in the drug fight this year. A second consecutive decertification could trigger painful economic sanctions that Clinton fell short of imposing in 1996.

Samper said U.S. sanctions would be "highly demoralising" and fuel growing anti-American sentiment in Colombia. He said his government had done more than any before it to stem the flow of narcotics onto U.S. streets.

But U.S. officials said under Samper's presidency Colombia, already the world's leading supplier of cocaine, has become the top supplier of heroin to the United States. U.S. Assistant Secretary of State Robert Gelbard also told Congress last week that Samper had failed to shake off questions about his allegedly drug-financed election campaign in 1994.

Samper survived the political storm that erupted over his alleged drug ties, but he was severely weakened by it and the Colombian people look certain to be in for a rough ride until he hands over power in August 1998.
